system:
You are a computational scientist who builds mechanistic models of biochemical and pharmacological processes from experimental data. Work the way a careful scientist does:

1. Plan: call write_plan first with a short list of steps; update it if your approach changes.
2. Look before you fit: inspect the data and use run_python for quick numeric checks that discriminate mechanisms (for example rates by inhibitor level, dose-normalised concentrations, effect against concentration over time).
3. Retrieve: search the mechanism library and read the relevant cards. They give equations, data signatures, pitfalls and the library model name to fit.
4. Hypothesise: record at least two competing hypotheses with record_hypothesis, each with what it predicts in these data. Update their status as evidence comes in.
5. Test: fit competing models with the same error model and compare BIC, residual diagnostics and identifiability. Fit independent models in the same turn to save steps.
6. Revise: if every candidate leaves structured residuals, the true mechanism may be missing from the library. Work out what the data do that no candidate allows, write a custom model, and test it.
7. Stay honest: always consider the simplest model, including no effect at all. Report parameters the data cannot determine. Never state a number that did not come from a tool result.
8. Submit with submit_model, citing fit_ids (and card ids you read) as evidence.

You have at most 20 model turns, so be efficient.
task_prompt:
A single IV bolus dose (mg) was given at t=0 and plasma concentration C (mg/L) was measured at times t (h), at two dose levels. Assays have roughly proportional (multiplicative) error.

The data table has 18 rows with columns: dose, t, C. Your model will be used to predict concentrations after a 500 mg dose.

Find the mechanistic model that best explains these data, fit it, check it critically, and submit it.

content.thinking:
I'm comparing normalized concentrations across the two doses at matching times. At 200 the early values run higher (2.24 vs 1.89 at 0.25h), but by 4h they nearly match, and later the 200 dose sits a bit lower (0.53 vs 0.63 at 12h), which makes me wonder whether elimination is saturable.

The higher dose now looks like it clears faster at the later times, which is the reverse of what Michaelis-Menten saturation would predict. Noise is probably around 10-15%, so I'll fit one- and two-compartment models plus an MM model to see which holds up.

content.text: Dose-normalised values are roughly superimposable, with some scatter. Fitting the one-compartment, two-compartment and Michaelis-Menten models with proportional error.

content.thinking:
I'm comparing the candidate models by BIC, where the one-compartment model comes out best, ahead of Michaelis-Menten and the two-compartment fit. Michaelis-Menten looks poorly identified, since Vmax and Km are weakly determined and Km sits near 40 even with doses up to 200, so I'm wondering whether the data is only partly saturated.

Michaelis-Menten doesn't hold up here: its ΔBIC of 2.3 favors the linear model despite the extra parameters, and the two-compartment fit collapses to one compartment. So I'll submit the one-compartment model and note the competing hypotheses briefly.

input.evidence: fit1: CL=4.955, V=48.8, all SEs ~3%, BIC -76.47, no residual structure; dose-normalised curves overlap across 50 and 200 mg.
fit3: Vmax and Km unidentifiable (SE ~140%, r=+1.000), fit collapses toward linear; BIC -74.2 is worse than linear -76.47 with one extra parameter.
fit2: distribution parameters run to the linear limit (Q≈0, V2≈21940), CL/Q perfectly correlated; BIC -70.69, worst.

input.summary: A one-compartment IV bolus model with linear elimination fits all 18 points with proportional error (sigma 0.108), CL 4.96 and V 48.8 (about 3% SE each), and no residual structure by dose or time (fit1). Dose-normalised concentrations overlap across the 50 and 200 mg doses. Michaelis-Menten elimination (fit3) has unidentifiable Vmax and Km and a worse BIC, and the two-compartment model (fit2) collapses to the one-compartment limit with a worse BIC, so both are rejected.
